title: The Tetris effect
hook: Play enough Tetris and you start seeing falling blocks when you close your eyes.
peek: After long sessions of Tetris, many players see falling pieces as they drift off to sleep, or catch themselves fitting real objects together in their heads. Researchers have studied it seriously.
lede: Play Tetris for hours and something odd can happen. You close your eyes at night and the pieces keep falling. Walking down the street, you notice how the buildings would slot together. The name was popularised by a 1994 Wired article, and scientists have since used the game to study how the brain replays what it has been practising.

bullets.text: Tetris was created by Alexey Pajitnov in Moscow in 1984. Its simple, repetitive shapes make it ideal for this kind of mental echo. It spread from computer to computer before reaching the West.
In 2000, the Harvard sleep researcher had people play Tetris for several days. Many reported seeing pieces as they fell asleep, including a few people with amnesia who could not remember playing.
These pictures on the edge of sleep are common. Stickgold's work suggested the brain may be replaying recent experience while memories settle.
Researchers have collected similar reports from many games: players hearing sound effects or seeing health bars in daily life. Most are brief and harmless.
Once something is on your mind, you notice it more. The frequency illusion is a waking cousin of the Tetris effect.

People who spend a long day skiing, rowing or on a boat often feel the motion continue that night. It is a very old version of the same thing. Sailors have long described still feeling the swell for hours after stepping ashore.
